description:
We are a passionate and innovation-driven team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, taking on the challenge “Dancing with the SARs.” Our mission is to transform complex Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from the NASA–ISRO NISAR mission into meaningful, interactive, and easy-to-understand visual insights.

Our vision is simple: Decode the signals from space, visualize Earth's changing rhythm, and turn scientific data into meaningful impact.
summary:
Brahmaputra FloodWatch is an interactive satellite-based water and flood-change monitoring platform developed for the Brahmaputra River Basin in Assam, India. It uses NASA–ISRO NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations to analyze water extent and identify changes between observation dates, including during cloudy conditions when optical satellite imagery may be limited.

The platform currently demonstrates two study areas: single-date water classification in Majuli and a two-date water-change comparison in Barpeta. It processes radar backscatter data using speckle filtering, adaptive thresholding, and spatial analysis, then presents the resulting information through an interactive web map, observation timeline, and comparison views.

By making radar-derived information easier to explore, Brahmaputra FloodWatch aims to support awareness of changing water conditions and demonstrate how satellite observations can contribute to flood monitoring and regional decision support.
details:
What the project does

Brahmaputra FloodWatch is a web-based geospatial analysis platform that demonstrates how Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations from the NASA–ISRO NISAR mission can be used to examine water extent and changes in water distribution in the Brahmaputra River Basin.

The project currently includes two study areas:

1. Majuli, Assam – Single-date water classification

The Majuli module analyzes a NISAR S-band Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance (GCOV) observation acquired on 27 August 2026. It uses the HHHH analysis layer to classify water and non-water areas. The processing workflow includes adaptive Lee speckle filtering, adaptive bimodal Otsu thresholding, and morphological minimum-mapping-unit processing. The output is presented as a geospatial water-classification layer.

2. Barpeta, Assam – Two-date water-change comparison

The Barpeta module compares two NISAR S-band observations: 27 June 2026 (baseline) and 9 July 2026 (event observation). The workflow analyzes changes in radar backscatter and classifies areas that changed from non-water to water according to the project's processing thresholds. The resulting comparison is displayed through map layers and observation information.

These outputs are algorithmic classifications based on the selected observations and processing method. They are not presented as official NISAR flood products or independently validated flood measurements.

How the platform works

The workflow begins with NISAR satellite data products. The selected radar data is processed into geospatial layers, analyzed using Python-based image-processing workflows, and made available through a FastAPI backend. A React web application communicates with the backend to display the study areas, observation information, map layers, and temporal comparison results.

Benefits and intended impact

Flooding and changing water conditions can affect communities, agriculture, infrastructure, and ecosystems across the Brahmaputra floodplain. SAR is useful because radar observations can be acquired during both day and night and are less affected by cloud cover than conventional optical imagery.

The project aims to make satellite-derived water information easier to explore, demonstrate the practical use of NISAR observations, and provide a foundation for further regional flood-monitoring and decision-support applications.

Technology used

  • Satellite data: NASA–ISRO NISAR S-band GCOV observations.
  • Programming: Python and JavaScript.
  • Frontend: React and Vite.
  • Backend: FastAPI.
  • Geospatial processing: HDF5 and GeoTIFF-based raster processing and geospatial analysis.
  • Deployment: Vercel for the frontend and Render for the backend.
  • Source-code management: Git and GitHub.

Creativity and design considerations

The project combines satellite radar observations, geospatial image processing, and an interactive web interface in one platform. Instead of presenting only raw satellite imagery, it turns selected observations into map-based water classifications and date-to-date comparisons. The team considered regional relevance, observation dates, data availability, processing limitations, and the importance of communicating algorithmic results without overstating their scientific validation.
